documents.abstract: This chapter examines how learning designers (LDs) mediate and lead assessment transformation in higher education in response to the rise of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). Drawing on cross-institutional interviews with 11 LDs from six Australian and New Zealand universities, it identifies ways that LDs are enacting their roles in response to GenAI: agents of change; emotional and cultural navigators; strategic influencers and policy shapers; designers of assessment; technical specialists and tool curators; and advocates for equity and inclusion. Situated within Whitchurch’s notion of the third space , LDs act as boundary spanners who translate institutional imperatives and academic values into coherent pedagogical practice. Their work supports transforming institutional ‘AI shock’ into opportunities for innovation, embedding authentic, reflective, and inclusive assessment practices. The chapter argues that LDs’ relational and strategic expertise is valuable in reimagining assessment for an AI-mediated educational future and calls for their recognition as co-leaders in shaping policy, pedagogy, and institutional culture.

This study examines how scientists in interdisciplinary programs learn from one another during collaboration. Researchers who participated in large scale research projects on human-AI teaming were surveyed about their collaborative experiences. Survey results show that regular cross-team meetings, careful listening, and adaptive communication are central to effective integration, while terminology conflicts and coordination costs persist. Findings highlight interaction structures and integrative roles as key levers for improving interdisciplinary teamwork. Framed within the context of the science of team science, the discussion highlights the support needed for interdisciplinary structures and processes enabling effective scientific collaboration.

Robot foundation models increasingly rely on flow-based action generation for general-purpose manipulation, yet the generated actions are not guaranteed to satisfy physical constraints such as joint limits and collision avoidance. This problem is especially challenging when the feasible set cannot be described analytically and is accessible only through black-box feasibility oracles. We study this practical oracle-only setting and propose an oracle-guided differentiable safeguard for safe flow-matching robot policies. The safeguard uses binary feasibility queries to correct unsafe updates in the forward pass, while extracting local boundary information to provide constraint-aware learning signals in the backward pass. Combined with discrete-time flow matching, the same safeguard is used during training and inference, enabling forward--backward aligned policy learning without explicit or differentiable constraint models. Experiments on obstacle-aware robotic manipulation demonstrate 100% constraint satisfaction while preserving task performance.

Abstract Courts are adopting artificial intelligence faster than lawmakers are writing rules for it. Risk scores inform bail and sentencing, language models draft summaries and sometimes reasoning, and judicial councils issue guidance in the absence of statutes. This article asks what a litigant is legally entitled to when an AI system touches the decision that affects them. Using a doctrinal and functional comparative method, we examine binding and soft-law instruments from the European Union, the Council of Europe, the United Kingdom, the United States, Brazil, Colombia and India, checked against official or reliable sources as of 26 October 2026. Three findings emerge. First, transparency duties are mostly addressed to institutions and regulators; the person whose liberty or rights are at stake rarely gets a right to know that AI was used, still less how. Second, human oversight is declared everywhere but engineered almost nowhere, despite strong evidence that nominal review produces automation bias rather than control. Third, remedies are the weakest link: with few exceptions, no instrument attaches a legal consequence to undisclosed or uncritical reliance on AI. We propose a Disclosure–Oversight–Remedy (DOR) framework that scales safeguards to the way AI is used, from auxiliary support to evaluative input, and prohibits determinative use. The framework converts principles into enforceable procedural entitlements and offers a template for legislators, judicial councils and courts.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Systems such as The AI Scientist have shown that AI agents can carry out and write up research, but in those demonstrations humans chose the research area and selected the outputs to show. We study letting the AI formulate the research question itself, and we report every run. Our system gives an off-the-shelf coding agent an instruction document and two skills: one for formulating the question, in which the agent diverges from recent technologies into problems of other fields, screens its candidates for known failure modes and obtains a critique from a different model; and one for peer review, in which a reviewer from another model family reruns the study from its records before the agent revises the paper. Over 13 development runs, changes to the one or two sentences that set the research area coincided with large shifts in what the candidate questions and the chosen papers were about, which led us to the area of a new technology applied to a societal problem. We froze the system after a pilot run and report five consecutive runs: the pilot, counted by a disclosed amendment to the pre-registration, and four pre-registered runs. All five runs went from question formulation to a revised, re-computable paper, with local computation on a laptop and no research input from humans, and external AI reviewers reading only the papers judged them at or near workshop level. We release the system, the five papers and the records needed to reproduce them.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Introduction Deep-space missions will progressively limit real-time ground support, rapid evacuation and resupply, creating a need for medical capabilities that can operate with graded autonomy. Artificial intelligence (AI) may support this transition, but terrestrial performance cannot be equated with spaceflight readiness. Methods We conducted a narrative, hypothesis-generating review of literature relevant to AI-enabled space healthcare. Sources were selected iteratively for their contribution to health monitoring, biofluid analysis, medical imaging, clinical decision support or radiation assessment. The review did not use a systematic screening protocol or formal meta-analytic quality assessment; therefore, findings are synthesised qualitatively and claims are calibrated to evidence maturity. Results Evidence was grouped as spaceflight operational use, space-relevant prototype or analogue demonstration, terrestrial clinical validation, terrestrial experimental demonstration, or conceptual transfer. AI may support personalised monitoring, biofluid interpretation, ultrasound acquisition and analysis, radiation forecasting and clinical decision support. However, most cited applications remain terrestrial demonstrations. Key barriers include limited astronaut data, shifted physiological baselines, restricted computation and power, sensor and storage constraints, model drift, explainability, uncertainty management and failure handling. Conclusion AI is most plausibly deployed as one component of an integrated autonomous medical system that combines wearables and biosensors, onboard records, imaging, radiation monitoring, clinical decision support, crew oversight and delayed telemedical consultation. Near-term priorities are prospective validation in mission-relevant analogues, personalised baselines, resource-aware edge deployment, explicit uncertainty thresholds, human override and pre-defined safe fallback procedures. AI should augment rather than replace telemedicine and professional judgement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) systems increasingly support decision-making across critical domains, yet explainable AI (XAI) approaches prioritise algorithmic transparency over human comprehension. While XAI reveals computational processes for model validation, end users require explanations integrating domain knowledge, contextual reasoning, and professional frameworks. This disconnect reveals a design challenge: existing approaches fail to address how practitioners need to understand and act upon AI recommendations. This paper introduces Explanatory AI as an emerging complementary paradigm where AI systems leverage generative and multimodal capabilities to serve as explanatory partners for human understanding. Unlike traditional XAI, which answers ‘How did the algorithm decide?’ for validation purposes, Explanatory AI addresses ‘Why does this make sense?’ for practitioners making informed decisions. Through theory-informed design, we synthesise multidisciplinary perspectives from cognitive science, communication research, and education with empirical evidence from healthcare and AI expert interviews. Our analysis identifies five dimensions distinguishing Explanatory AI from XAI: explanatory purpose, communication mode, epistemic stance, adaptivity, and cognitive design. We derive five meta-requirements and formulate ten design principles prescribing how to build such systems, illustrated through five UI mockups exemplifying implementation. Explanatory AI operates standalone or combined with XAI, serving distinct purposes in creating systems that genuinely support human reasoning and decision-making.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Few-Shot Action Recognition (FSAR) widely use in Action Recognition domains with limited labeled data, such as medical surgery. Existing FSAR methods often rely on single-modal approaches, which suffer from limited feature representation and a lack of semantic understanding. To overcome these limitations, we propose MoMA, a novel Mamba-based multimodal FSAR framework, designed to optimize the learning of multimodal information and improve the performance of few-shot action recognition tasks. MoMA integrates a multimodal large language model (MLLM) to generate semantically rich representations from both textual and video data, which are then aligned and fused with visual features. To address the challenges of domain-specific prior knowledge and intra-class variance, we introduce a dual-branch contrastive learning architecture that reinforces category distinctions and mitigates the accumulation of intra-class heterogeneity. Our experimental results show that MoMA outperforms state-of-the-art methods on the HMDB51, Kinetics, and SSv2 datasets, achieving improvements of 1.5%, 1.9%, and 3.5%, respectively, in the 1-shot setting.

The rising pressure on lifestyle related illnesses including obesity, diabetes and heart diseases, has heightened pressure on the need to develop digital health solutions in an intelligent and scalable manner. The paper describes LiveFit, which is AI-enhanced customized nutrition and subscription-based health management software, which combines real-time monitoring of macronutrients, automatically adjusted diet, online ordering of meal plans, and an interface available across platforms. The suggested system adheres to a layered structure, which comprises a web-based dashboard, a Node.js-based microservice configuration and the MongoDB Atlas cloud storage, as well as a React Native (Expo Router) application. JWT-based authentication is used to ensure secure communication and brings scaling to data processing and user interactions which are facilitated by cloud-hosted APIs. The system will integrate the logic of contextual recommendation which dynamically examines nutritional intake and gives personal feedback in terms of perceived deficiencies. In contrast to other traditional calorie counting programs, LiveFit is aimed at active nutritional evaluation and dynamic intervention as opposed to passive dieting over a record. Experimental analysis proves the stable system operation, average API response time does not exceed 200 ms, and the accuracy of authentication is stable with as much as multi-user dependence. The suggested framework identifies the possibility to use artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, and subscription-based models to provide adaptive and scalable preventive healthcare systems.

Long-run RTL simulation of CPU candidates can take hours, while short diagnostic runs may miss performance degradation that emerges later in execution. This evaluation cost can delay design decisions in LLM-agent-based CPU development. We present a development environment in which LLM agents implement CPU candidates on an FPGA and use on-board performance measurements to guide design decisions. We applied it to the human-supervised development of a single-cycle RV32I core into a three-wide out-of-order RV32IM core. The final design reaches 5.61 CoreMark/MHz at 130 MHz on a Artix-7 FPGA. For the same CPU candidate running 8,000 CoreMark iterations, FPGA evaluation, including implementation, was 9.6x faster than single-threaded RTL simulation. In one case, board measurements revealed long-run performance degradation in a candidate that improved in a short diagnostic run. The result guided candidate selection and led to RTL-based root-cause analysis and a fix.

Personalized fine-tuning of Large Language Models (LLMs) enhances user experience but incurs substantial computational costs. Recent studies show that initializing training from a style-similar fine-tuned model reduces adaptation overhead, turning such checkpoints into reusable, tradable assets. A marketplace for these checkpoints, however, faces information asymmetry: sellers may misreport a checkpoint's style, while buyers cannot verify its usefulness before purchase, which invites adverse selection. We introduce LLM eBay, a simple single-round marketplace for trading fine-tuned LLMs. Sellers are paid per purchase at a posted price, and a truncated quadratic proper scoring rule adjusts each payment according to how well the seller's style report agrees with a style signal that the platform measures by generating text on hidden prompts. We show that the score elicits the verifier's expected signal, characterize exactly when truthful reporting is a seller best response under per-purchase demand, and bound the downside risk from noisy verification. In an end-to-end study with real LoRA checkpoints on two base models and three buyer tasks, LLM eBay reduces measured convergence steps by 8.5\% relative to retrieval over self-reported style (95\% CI [1.0\%, 15.9\%]). In model-based market simulations built on a measured style-to-cost relationship, it cuts style-claim error by 96.5\% (from 0.424 to 0.015), recovers 96.3\% of Oracle welfare, saves 72.4\% of the cost of fine-tuning from the base model, and keeps all providers profitable in the default setting.

Robotic navigation typically assumes a collision-free route to the goal exists; in cluttered environments with movable obstacles, however, reaching the goal may require physical interaction. Classical solutions encode these behaviors through geometric rules and task-specific logic, while learning-based approaches often constrain the decision space to low-dimensional motion commands or predefined action sets. We instead consider a broader decision space, jointly selecting the skill, relevant object, and geometric target. Our language-conditioned task planner, fine-tuned with LoRA on synthetic data, maps natural-language tasks and a structured scene representation to variable-length sequences of parameterized actions, executed by low-level reinforcement-learning policies. The planner learns the geometric relations underlying interactive navigation and outperforms a classical planner and a prompted frontier model on interactive navigation tasks. Comparisons with models trained from scratch indicate that composition does not require pretraining when the representation is structured, whereas pretraining yields more reliable geometric targets. At the low level, we introduce an end-to-end whole-body planar pushing policy that achieves a 93.3% success rate in simulation, versus 83.5% for a hierarchical baseline, while reducing completion time by more than 60%. On hardware, the hierarchy yields the correct skill composition in 44/45 trials and end-to-end success in 34/45. Project website: https://anonymousprojects-dev.github.io/LLM-guided-LocoManipulation-Quadrupeds/

Deep infiltrating endometriosis (DIE) is a severe form of endometriosis characterized by deep infiltration of endometriotic tissue into the retroperitoneal space and muscular walls of pelvic organs. Its nonspecific clinical presentation and the limited sensitivity of standard diagnostic methods contribute to significant diagnostic delays, while current treatments are primarily symptomatic and associated with high recurrence rates. This review summarizes current and emerging approaches to the diagnosis of DIE, including molecular markers, high-resolution imaging techniques, standardized protocols and classifications, and artificial intelligence-based algorithms. Potential therapeutic targets involved in the pathogenesis of DIE are discussed, including the PI3K/Akt/mTOR signaling pathway, microRNAs, fibrogenic factors, and specific immune mechanisms. Particular attention is given to multidisciplinary rehabilitation strategies, such as physiotherapy, exercise, nutritional and psychological support, and modulation of the vaginal and gut microbiota. Further advances in the diagnosis, treatment, and rehabilitation of patients with DIE are needed to facilitate earlier diagnosis, enable personalized therapy, and improve long-term clinical outcomes.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) systems -predominantly deep convolutional neural networks (CNN), and more recently vision transformers (ViT) and vision–language models have been applied extensively to fracture detection on plain radiographs. As primary studies have proliferated, numerous systematic reviews and meta-analyses have appeared, each pooling overlapping sets of primary studies and reaching conclusions that are not always concordant. The lower limb comprising the hip and proximal femur, femoral shaft and distal femur, knee and patella, tibia and fibula, ankle, and foot is clinically important and heterogeneous: some regions such as the hip and ankle are comparatively well studied, whereas others such as the foot, patella, and isolated fibula fractures are under-represented in the review-level literature. An umbrella review - a systematic synthesis of existing systematic reviews rather than of primary studies is the appropriate design to map this fragmented evidence base, characterise its consistency, quantify overlap between reviews, and appraise the methodological quality of the reviews themselves. This protocol specifies, in advance, the objectives, eligibility criteria, search strategy, appraisal instruments, data-extraction framework, overlap assessment, and synthesis plan, in order to minimise post-hoc decision-making and to support transparent, reproducible conduct. Status at registration: searches are complete (August to October 2026); title and abstract screening is in progress, having commenced on 16 October 2026; full-text screening and data extraction have not begun. This registration is therefore submitted for research that is underway, with the current state disclosed.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Machine learning (ML) is increasingly used to predict the factor of safety (FoS) and stability state of slopes, often combined with explainable artificial intelligence (XAI). This PRISMA 2020 systematic review searched OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref (2000–2026), screened 6,550 unique records, mapped 1,009 eligible studies at abstract level and synthesised 137 open-access full texts. Publications grew sharply after 2020, and artificial neural networks are giving way to tree ensembles, deep learning and metaheuristic hybrids. Reported performance is high (median test 2 0.97; median accuracy 0.93) but rests mainly on synthetic limit-equilibrium or finite-element data (51 % of studies) or on small, overlapping compilations of published case histories (median 190 cases). Only 11 % of studies addressed data quality or duplicates, 39 % used cross-validation, 4 % validated on independent cases and 15 % shared code or data. Class thresholds ranged from FoS 1.0 to 1.3. About half of the studies reported explanations, mostly feature importance, sensitivity analysis or SHAP, but none validated them quantitatively against limit-equilibrium sensitivities. Priorities are curated public datasets, leakage-aware and external validation, explicit target definitions, uncertainty quantification and mechanics-based validation of explanations. Key Words: slope stability, factor of safety, machine learning, explainable artificial intelligence, systematic review, PRISMA

Artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing experience design, process coordination, and strategic identity communication in organizations. Whereas there has been a trend in brand-related research focusing on the impact of AI-based personalization, automation, and customer interaction, change management research has mainly concentrated on digital transformation, adaptability, and capability development. However, little research connects the topic of organizational changes in AI with brand renewal. Thus, this paper bridges this gap through developing and demonstrating an integrated framework for managing AI-based brand transformation in Indian organizations. Building on ADKAR model, dynamic capabilities theory, agile change management, digital transformation maturity, internal branding, employee brand ambassadorship, and the AI-revised Brand Identity Prism developed by Kapferer, this paper puts forward the AI-Brand Change Framework (ABCF). In addition to the theoretical progress, in the manuscript an agent-based simulation is provided in which 168 diverse organizational agents are developed based on the framework’s causal logic. The simulation is a test of theoretical consistency, not an empirical test. Internally consistent and implementable, the framework suggests that digital sophistication, adaptive capabilities, nimble change management, ADKAR congruence, internal brand stewardship, employee brand advocacy, and AI-driven brand recognition correlate positively with brand rejuvenation in the simulated agent cohort. The study contributes to the knowledge by linking the concepts of branding and change management, applying the theory of internal branding within the framework of AI-driven situations and proposing an operational model for organizations undergoing AI-driven transformation. The research also includes a step-by-step guide to implementation, a diagnostic tool with indicative KPIs and policy recommendations for Indian businesses.

Artificial intelligence in education (AIED) has expanded rapidly since the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, yet recent development remains insufficiently mapped. This study examines publication growth, thematic change, citation impact, journal profiles and collaboration structure in AI-related research published in four selected journals between 2020 and 2025: Interactive learning environments (ILE), Computers and education: artificial intelligence (CAEAI), Journal of learning analytics (JLA) and International journal of artificial intelligence in education (IJAIED). Because three venues also publish broader educational technology research, 2719 Scopus records were screened using an explicit AI-relevance criterion; 1397 publications were retained and 1322 excluded. AI-relevant output rose from 54 publications in 2020 to 558 in 2025, a 10.3-fold increase and 59.5% compound annual growth rate. Eight predefined lexical themes matched 60.3% of the corpus and therefore provide lower-bound counts; generative AI and large language models grew from 1 publication in 2020–2021 to 307 in 2024–2025 and recorded the largest count among the eight themes. Keyword clustering placed generative AI in the motor-theme quadrant. Co-authorship analysis identified a fragmented prolific core of 74 authors in the largest connected component, divided into eight sub-groups and linked by authors with high betweenness centrality. The findings characterize AI-related literature in these four journals rather than the AIED field as a whole, and the observed growth is temporally associated with, but not shown to be caused by, the release of ChatGPT.

Background: AI is increasingly examined as a tool for science-specific instruction, feedback, inquiry and teacher preparation, but research designs and claimed outcomes vary. Methods: This systematic literature review applied PRISMA 2020 reporting to a title-only Scopus search through Watase Uake on 5 September 2026. Two phrases retrieved 123 and 114 raw records, respectively (237 total). Searches were restricted to Q1 journal publications dated 2023–2026. The initial selection retained 49 articles; eight were removed in a subsequent science-education relevance audit. Two further Q1-indexed Scopus reports identified outside the Watase export were assessed but excluded as unrelated plant-science research. The final corpus comprised 41 articles, synthesized descriptively and thematically with study designs differentiated. Results: The literature describes AI as a scaffold for inquiry, dialogic science reasoning, multimodal representation, feedback, learning analytics and science-teacher preparation. Some primary studies report context-dependent benefits for measured learning outcomes, but findings cannot be generalized across heterogeneous designs. Conclusions: Appropriate science-specific pedagogy, human–AI interaction, teacher competence and ethical oversight are central considerations.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged. Hierarchical Semantic Traces preserve realized operations and dependencies for reproducible comparisons of legal release constraints at fixed work. Task-linked measurements connect these workloads to serving execution and GPU/NPU hardware behavior, revealing why serving efficiency does not always translate into timely task completion. The benchmark code is available at https://github.com/ShengxuanQiu/MAServeBench.

The importance of the psychometric properties of measures in applied and basic research in the social sciences, particularly in psychology, seems to have increased with the widespread access to these procedures and their growing dissemination worldwide. Nonetheless, the availability and use of these measures may be problematic for researchers. In this paper, we propose the concept of measurement validity induction as a conceptual tool to describe the omission or inappropriate application of measurement validity results obtained in one context to justify the use and interpretation of the same measures in different contexts. In general, this involves the risk of using irrelevant information to justify the use or interpretation of a measure, that is, advocating for validity when it may not exist. Several examples from the published literature on scale validations are analyzed to detect measurement validity induction in the areas of clinical practice, occupational health, and user satisfaction. With this definition (measurement validity induction), we argue for the need to report minimum parameters of the validity of a measure in a new context beyond those reported in manuals or previous studies.

Research materials for the study of core and peripheral departure in independent games. This retrospective archive preserves versioned codebooks and reference cards, machine-coding inputs and outputs, audit records, and analysis scripts. It distinguishes the v8 calibration and 600-work seeded-subset analyses from historical experiments and later LLM coder-simulation probes. Original machine records retain their provenance and are not relabeled as independent human validation.

It has all but become a cliché now to say that the proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) presents significant challenges to assessment practices in higher education. While concerns about academic integrity have dominated the discourse to date, these new technologies have introduced a broader range of assessment issues that require addressing. In this chapter, we argue that the focus should transition from detecting academic dishonesty to reconsidering what student learning is and how it might be inferred through assessment. Validity and security remain essential components of accountable and trustworthy assessment regimes in a time of AI. However, the emergence of GenAI and AI agents necessitates renewed attention to learning processes in addition to outcomes. Assumptions about what can and should be measured, and what criteria are appropriate, must evolve as learning processes transform in response to AI integration. This chapter argues for the need to address questions of measurement validity before considering how assessment can be implemented to make more accurate inferences about learning in environments where AI tools function as collaborative partners in the educational experience rather than merely as potential avenues for academic misconduct.

Abstract Protein oxidation (PO) is a major biochemical process in meat, affecting color, texture, water-holding capacity, digestibility, flavor, and safety. This review integrates the molecular mechanisms of meat protein oxidation, including free-radical chain reactions, metal-catalyzed Fenton chemistry, lipid–protein crosstalk, and enzymatic pathways. It discusses how direct ROS/RNS attack and secondary aldehyde adduction cause structural and functional damage, with dose-, matrix-, pH-, and temperature-dependent effects that can be beneficial at mild levels but detrimental when excessive. Health implications of dietary oxidized proteins are critically evaluated, distinguishing biomarker associations, animal-model mechanisms, and limited human causal evidence. Natural antioxidants, encapsulation, nonthermal processing, and combined strategies are assessed for controlling oxidation. Advanced analytical and artificial intelligence -based approaches are also highlighted. Finally, key knowledge gaps and future directions are outlined to support precise quality and safety management in muscle foods.

This thesis examines the role, capabilities, and significance of monitoring the learning process through digital learning platforms in improving the quality of education. It discusses mechanisms for tracking students’ learning activities, analyzing academic performance indicators, assessing independent learning activities, and making pedagogical decisions based on the collected data. Furthermore, the potential of Learning Analytics, automated assessment, individualized feedback, and artificial intelligence technologies in improving digital monitoring systems is explored.

Rapid solar photovoltaic (PV) grid integration requires robust global maximum power point tracking (GMPPT) under partial shading conditions (PSCs). Traditional continuous reinforcement learning (RL) controllers rely on static hyperparameters, rendering them susceptible to local peak trapping and power oscillations during rapid environmental transients. To resolve these computational and dynamic limitations, this paper presents a meta-learning-based reinforcement learning framework featuring an adaptive meta-deep deterministic policy gradient (AM-DDPG) controller for simultaneous GMPPT and automated voltage regulation in grid-connected PV systems. The core algorithmic novelty is an outer meta-learning layer governed by meta-plasticity principles that dynamically tunes the inner DDPG agent’s hyperparameters through a power–duty-cycle sensitivity gradient. To bridge advanced artificial intelligence with physical hardware safety standards, a deterministic override layer strictly clamps intermediate DC-link voltage fluctuations within safe operating limits (500 V–600 V). A grid-forming (GFM) inverter stage completes the system, providing autonomous synchronization through decentralized droop mechanisms. Evaluated under complex, time-varying, real-world shading profiles, the AM-DDPG framework consistently achieves 99.4%-99.8% tracking efficiency, converges within 12 ms, and suppresses the steady-state DC-link voltage ripple by 62% compared with conventional DDPG. These findings highlight a safe, computationally efficient AI control solution for resilient energy extraction in modern power grids.

European cities increasingly use digital platforms, predictive analytics and artificial intelligence to allocate welfare, regulate mobility, plan public space and support security. This article examines how these systems reshape migrants’ effective enjoyment of freedom of religion or belief. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, informed by interdisciplinary scholarship, it connects European human-rights law, EU data-protection and equality law, the Artificial Intelligence Act, and scholarship on urban religious diversity. The analysis identifies three recurring risks: the digital invisibility of minority religious needs in planning and service design; proxy and intersectional discrimination in welfare, housing, education and integration systems; and chilling effects produced by biometric and data-intensive surveillance of religious dress, assembly and worship. Documented institutional practices and adjudicated cases are expressly distinguished from hypothetical legal stress tests used to identify foreseeable pathways of rights interference. The article also shows that urban technology can improve access, coordination and participation when governed through transparent, accessible and contestable procedures. It proposes a rights-based model centred on infrastructural neutrality, religion-sensitive impact assessment, participatory co-design, data minimisation, meaningful explanation, accountable human review and effective remedies. It argues that religious freedom in the algorithmic city depends not only on the legality of individual decisions, but also on the design and governance of the digital infrastructures through which urban membership is recognised and administered. The European focus is methodologically deliberate: the Council of Europe and EU systems supply distinct yet interacting standards for digitally mediated municipal action. The article specifies when a technological disadvantage engages Article 9 ECHR rather than principally privacy, equality or administrative law, differentiates risks by migration status, and tests the proposed principle against two legally bounded institutional examples.

Audio descriptions (AD) are essential for making visual media accessible to blind and low-vision (BLV) users. While Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) offer a scalable solution for generating audio descriptions on-demand, their performance on ``inline'' audio descriptions -- which must fit within existing silences in a video -- remains under-explored, particularly for diverse user-generated content (UGC). We present a comprehensive investigation into MLLM-generated inline audio descriptions. First, we introduce MTG-AD, a professionally annotated dataset of 36 hours of videos, each averaging $\sim$5 mins. and 8k+ descriptions in total, co-created by paired blind and sighted AD professionals to provide a high-quality benchmark for this task. Second, we propose MTG-AD-Eval, an evaluation framework based on audio description expert guidelines that provides fine-grained, reference-free actionable metrics for model improvement. Crucially, our framework evaluates the end-to-end task: it renders the generated scripts into audio tracks to assess their fit within the original video's natural silences, minimizing disruptive overlaps. Our analysis across frontier MLLMs reveals that while models accurately describe visual events and substantially reduce speech overlaps, gaps persist in narrative pacing and flow. Finally, we empirically validate that our automated and reference-free metrics correlate significantly with human quality ratings from sighted raters and 7 BLV participants, finding that while users narrowly prefer human-authored audio descriptions, they find MLLM-generated audio descriptions highly beneficial for comprehension. We provide actionable system design guidance and release MTG-AD at https://hf.co/datasets/google/mind-the-gap-inline-ad and MTG-AD-Eval at https://github.com/google/mtg-ad.

While mining parallel sentences from web pages has proven effective for low-resource machine translation, the majority of the world's languages have little to no web presence. What they do have, though, are resources that are the result of centuries of efforts by linguists, such as grammars, dictionaries, and other documentation materials. We propose extracting translation examples from such linguistic resources, which offer parallel data for languages under-represented online and could potentially scale to thousands more languages. We develop a pipeline to achieve this, leveraging an Optical Character Recognition (OCR) model as well as a vision language model (VLM), to ensure identified content to be aligned with visual layout information. We demonstrate the utility of the extracted bitexts for bootstrapping translation systems across 20 languages, both by training machine translation models and by applying in-context learning for large language models. For in-context learning, we observe improvements of +15.78 and +6.94 chrF2++ over zero-shot translation for into low- and high-resource languages, respectively.

Up to 40% of clinical candidates are poorly-soluble drugs, which rely heavily on nanoparticle formulations for oral and targeted delivery. Successful formulation largely depends on the co-assembly of drug and excipients into stable nanostructures. However, traditional wet-lab trial-and-error approaches require months, even years for discoveries to be made, with a substantial cost in raw materials. From research, there are 1440 high-throughput screening pairs of drug combination, but few AI algorithms have been applied to this task, especially with the rapidly evolving chemistry large language model (LLM), which hasn’t been evaluated on this task yet. Herein, I introduce the novel application of chemistry foundation model representations to drug-excipient nanoparticle co-assembly prediction. Specifically, this essay introduces MoBiTDE, a molecular bilinear two-tower network designed to learn pairwise compatibility between drugs and excipients. MoBiTDE employs frozen SMI-TED embeddings as pre-trained molecular representations, complemented by 24 RDKit-derived physicochemical descriptors. Drugs and excipient representations are processed through two independent molecular towers and coupled by a rank-32 bilinear interaction module to explicitly capture cross-molecular interactions. The resulting pairwise representation is subsequently fed into a single positive-weighted binary classification head for co-assembly prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that MoBiTDE outperforms other methods under different evaluation settings. Notably, its predictive performance further improves as the dataset expands, highlighting the potential of pre-trained molecular representations to benefit from increasing experimental data. In summary, MoBiTDE provides an effective framework for learning drug–excipient compatibility and offers a promising computational approach to facilitate the discovery of self-assembling nanoparticle formulations. It can improve drug discovery efficiency by reducing the number of trials, focusing only wet-lab testing on promising combinations.

Industry 4.0 research still treats sustainability, inclusivity, and workforce capability as separate concerns. This chapter proposes the Human Platform, a higher order sociotechnical capability through which technological enablement, inclusivity practices, and sustainability orientation jointly shape human adaptability and organizational performance. Drawing on Sociotechnical Systems Theory, Human Capital Theory, Dynamic Capabilities Theory, the Capability Approach, and Stakeholder Theory, the chapter develops the Human Platform Model and eight theoretical propositions linking these constructs to sustainable organizational outcomes. A proposed explanatory sequential mixed methods design is offered for future empirical validation, illustrated through documented industry cases. The chapter closes with implications for theory, management practice, and workforce policy in digitally transforming organizations.

In the age of artificial intelligence (AI), learning practices surge the environment. We are at a stage of critically processing how active learning practices are still relevant in the age of AI. This chapter will critically portray the field-based impact of AI in learning engagements by rationalising students’ active learning practices within the context of AI by discussing the right way of introducing AI in education, and how significant teachers’ roles are in the use of AI. Further to these arguments, an Australian case study will be briefly discussed to show how to effectuate learning experiences and maintain student agency in that learning process. This chapter should be seen as a thought-provoking piece on how to re-examine the active learning experience from a not-so-distant past called today and into the future in the age of dynamic AI.

Leukocyte count and differential are core indicators for clinical infection assessment, hematological disease diagnosis, and therapeutic monitoring. Currently, clinical testing heavily relies on automated hematology analyzers. Influenced by factors such as specimen characteristics, limited analyzer recognition capability, and improper manual operations, automated testing often produces unreliable results, interfering with clinical decision-making and threatening patient safety. Existing studies remain fragmented, lacking a multidimensional error-tracing framework and practical corrective strategies covering the entire testing workflow. A narrative review was conducted to summarize the causes, identification methods, and corrective strategies for unreliable leukocyte results. Relevant literature up to August 2026 was searched in PubMed/MEDLINE and CNKI. We categorized multidimensional error sources into specimen-related interferents, leukocyte morphological and developmental abnormalities, and preanalytical or systematic factors, and established a practical diagnostic workflow spanning from anomaly recognition to result reporting. By incorporating both legacy and current analytical systems, we compared the characteristic scattergram patterns of various interferents across analyzers with different detection principles, broadening the applicability to diverse clinical laboratories. To better ensure the reliability of corrective strategies and provide diverse alternative options, we not only summarized widely accepted routine practices but also included case-based experimental methods. The proposed multidimensional error-tracing system and practical diagnostic workflow significantly improve analytical accuracy and reduce clinical risks. However, current hematology analyzers cannot automatically identify or correct complex interferences. Future systems must integrate multi-platform advantages, optimize complex cell recognition capabilities, and enrich multidimensional scattergram information to overcome existing analytical limitations. Furthermore, integrating artificial intelligence technology holds immense potential to drive automated hematology analysis toward a more intelligent and precise direction.
topics: Clinical Laboratory Practices and Quality Control

documents.abstract: The advent of urbanization, mobility, and demands are shifting modern cities towards the implementation of intelligent technologies to offer safer, smoother, and sustainable transportation. The chapter explores the possibility of smart city infrastructure, along with IoT-enabled multimodal systems, to radically enhance traffic control and city surveillance using the assistance of drone-based capabilities. Traditional surveillance is not always effective in providing high-resolution and timely information, and the integration of UAVs with terrestrial sensors, edge cameras, and artificial intelligence can enable the optimization of traffic flow in real time, promptly identify incidents, and manage congestion flexibly. Advanced imaging, LiDAR, and communication units are added to the drones and offer a supplement to situational awareness by giving an aerial perspective. Multimodal data fusion architectures, scalable communication architecture, and intelligent decision-support systems are introduced in the chapter. The UAV-enabled systems have the potential to transform the field, which has been demonstrated by the most crucial applications, including emergency response, road safety assessment, and infrastructure monitoring. The problems of privacy, energy efficiency, and regulatory limitations are introduced, as well as the future research opportunities of resilient smart mobility ecosystems.

This review examines emerging applications of deep learning, multimodal data fusion, explainable artificial intelligence (XAI), and longitudinal severity tracking in canine dermatology. It critically synthesizes research published between 2021 and 2026, covering convolutional neural networks, EfficientNet, YOLO-based lesion detection, MobileNetV2, Vision Transformers, and the integration of clinical metadata with dermatological images. The review discusses the limitations of visual-only classification, including duplicate-image leakage, limited dataset diversity, insufficient external validation, and uncertainty in real-world clinical performance. It also examines explainability methods such as Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and SHAP, alongside the challenges of tracking lesion severity across repeated examinations. The paper proposes the PetZoe VetScan paradigm: a veterinarian-in-the-loop decision-support architecture combining lesion detection, multimodal clinical metadata, visual explanations, uncertainty estimation, and longitudinal comparison. The proposed system is intended to support preliminary screening and monitoring rather than replace professional veterinary diagnosis or clinical judgment. Its longitudinal severity-tracking component is identified as experimental and requires further validation. The review highlights research priorities including independent external validation, diverse clinical datasets, patient-level data splitting, standardized severity assessment, transparent uncertainty communication, and prospective clinical evaluation. Keywords: Canine dermatology; deep learning; explainable artificial intelligence; Grad-CAM; longitudinal lesion tracking; multimodal clinical decision support; veterinary artificial intelligence; veterinarian-in-the-loop.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The development of multimodal artificial intelligence has accelerated to such a degree that the integration of Natural Language Processing (NLP) and computer vision has become possible such that systems are able to interpret, reason over, and create cross-modal content in cooperation. Vision-Language Models (VLMs) can be seen as an important step in this development and, ironically, the CLIP and GPT-4V models are called Vision-Language Models because they align textual and visual representations in common embedding spaces and multimodal transformer architectures. These models help in zero-shot learning, cross-modal retrieval, visual question answering, caption generation, and multimodal reasoning, thus reducing AI capabilities from perception to contextual understanding. In the chapter, the theoretic, architectural design, and training paradigm of NLP-vision integration are explored. It also examines practical implementation in areas of healthcare diagnostics, intelligent surveillance systems, autonomous systems, e-commerce, accessibility technologies, and multimedia content analysis. Contrasting and generative multimodal methods are proven to be more beneficial in terms of accuracy, robustness, and contextual reasoning than unimodal baselines as experimentally evaluated. Moreover, the chapter includes computational, ethical, and scalability issues of implementing the use of large-scale VLMs. This publication makes a contribution to the future of AI-based multimedia and multimodal intelligence systems by offering a comprehensive framework on how researchers and practitioners should further develop algorithmic innovation in applied deployment strategies.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

documents.abstract: As the effects of climate change become increasingly apparent, the demand for renewable energy sources such as wind power continues to grow. However, renewables' variable and intermittent nature presents significant challenges in their integration into energy grids. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool to address these issues. Still, its adoption in the energy sector has been hindered by the opacity of many AI models, which often function as black boxes. This paper introduces a carefully adapted GradientSHAP approach to provide interpretability for multivariate, multistep wind power forecasting -- a largely underexplored area. This capability is critical for day-ahead grid management and, to the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to apply GradientSHAP in the context of wind power forecasting. To address the inherent dimensionality, we developed novel visualizations that deliver both local and global explanations, uncovering intricate relationships between environmental factors, site-specific conditions, and temporal dynamics. While GradientSHAP is not an out-of-the-box solution, our findings demonstrate that, with thoughtful handling of SHAP values and domain expertise, it can offer valuable insights into model behaviour, supporting more informed and trustworthy decision-making. Nevertheless, its complexity poses challenges for practical implementation. Future research should focus on streamlining these interpretability methods to make them more actionable for routine deployment in critical energy applications.

Museum-grounded generative-AI guides can extend heritage interpretation from information delivery to a participatory encounter that connects what visitors understand, experience, and intend to protect. Existing research, however, rarely distinguishes whether system affordances are associated with desirable outcomes, predictively important, or necessary for those outcomes to reach high levels. Drawing on the stimulus–organism–response framework, this study develops an integrated model of how dialogic, epistemic, social, cultural, adaptive, and participatory affordances relate to perceived heritage-value enhancement, flow, stewardship self-efficacy, and pro-heritage stewardship intention. Post-interaction evidence from adults reporting prior Jinghui use was examined through partial least squares structural equation modeling, artificial neural networks, a matched Basis-KAN predictive benchmark, and necessary-condition analysis. The findings identify outcome-specific profiles: responsive dialog is prominent for perceived value enhancement; visitor agency has the highest mean ANN importance for flow; epistemic transparency and cultural authenticity are closely ranked for self-efficacy; and perceived value enhancement and flow retain necessity evidence for stewardship intention. The direct value-enhancement–self-efficacy path is unsupported. Close coefficient differences do not establish superior design features, and ANN ranks vary across fitted runs. Comparison of nonlinear importance with held-out prediction further shows that a flexible representation does not automatically yield stronger predictive performance. By linking accountable system design to visitors’ meaning-making and stewardship motivation, this study provides an evidence-informed foundation for designing museum generative AI as public interpretive infrastructure that connects cultural accountability with informed participation in heritage stewardship.

This review examines the current literature on the application of atomic force microscopy (AFM) to cancer mechanophenotyping, with particular emphasis on cellular Young's modulus and its potential diagnostic significance. A structured electronic search of PubMed, Scopus and Google Scholar was conducted to identify studies published between 1999 and 2025 reporting AFM‐based measurements of cellular Young's modulus in cancer‐related models. Across multiple malignancies, reduced cellular stiffness is frequently observed in malignant compared with non‐malignant cells and is associated with cytoskeletal remodelling, increased deformability and altered cell–matrix interactions. However, the relationship between Young's modulus and malignancy is not universally monotonic. Nanomechanical properties may vary across different pathological states and malignant phenotypes rather than following a simple monotonic trajectory, while invasive and metastatic cells can dynamically remodel their cytoskeleton and modify their stiffness in response to environmental and mechanical constraints. Young's modulus should therefore not be regarded as an isolated universal cancer biomarker, but rather as one component of a dynamic mechanophenotype influenced by disease stage, cellular region, microenvironment and measurement methodology. Recent advances in automated force acquisition, optical cell recognition, artificial intelligence and high‐throughput AFM are beginning to address traditional limitations in measurement efficiency and operator dependence. The future diagnostic value of AFM may therefore lie in integrating Young's modulus with complementary parameters, including spatial mechanical heterogeneity, viscoelasticity, adhesion, deformation‐energy characteristics and nanotopography, to define multidimensional cancer mechanophenotypes. Standardised acquisition and analysis protocols, together with validation in patient‐derived specimens, will be essential for translating AFM nanomechanics from an experimental measurement into a clinically informative biomechanical biomarker.

The number of people experiencing mental health issues is increasing around the globe and the demand for effective technology-based solutions to tackle mental health challenges continues to increase. This research aims to conduct a systematic review of Natural Language Processing (NLP) techniques that have been used for the identification of emotions from conversations in the context of mobile applications for mental health support. The study has followed PRISMA guidelines for the examination of literature from the years 2017 to 2025 and categorisation of machine-learning, deep learning and transformer-based models including BERT, RoBERTa and Large Language Models (LLMs) for emotion recognition in mental health applications. The findings of the study show that transformer-based models provide the highest levels of accuracy in detecting depression, suicidal ideations and emotional distress, with an accuracy rate exceeding 90%, when applied to user generated inputs through NLP methods. Nonetheless, there are obstacles to the advancement of AI technologies for use within mental health support, including the high levels of computational power needed for mobile applications, insufficient explanations for the outputs of AI systems, and the lack of high-quality multilingual mental health data.

We introduce NEOPIC, a framework for learning the field operator in particle-based methods applied to kinetic plasma simulations. Its key novelty is a neural operator that acts directly on the empirical measure of the particles, rather than on a grid, and is evaluated at the particle positions. No mesh or tree is needed and, unlike grid-based neural operators, no deposition onto a mesh takes place, so the particle noise that dominates the inputs of particle simulations is not aliased. Since it replaces only the field solve, it serves as a plug-and-play field solver for particle-based methods: it can be trained on data from particle-in-cell, particle-in-Fourier or tree codes, and combined with any time integrator, including implicit schemes. We prove that the discrete evaluation coincides with the continuous operator at any number of particles (representation equivalence) and derive an error analysis that separates sampling, learning and time-stepping errors: up to the learning error, NEOPIC has the error structure of standard Monte Carlo particle methods. We show that the particle noise in the training data acts as an implicit regularizer, which gives guidance on the number of training particles in relation to the particle numbers used at inference. A complexity analysis shows that NEOPIC is an $O(N_p)$ method whose constants are set by the architecture alone, independently of any mesh or tree. Numerical experiments on electrostatic benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including Landau damping, two-stream and bump-on-tail instabilities, a cyclotron mini-app and a Penning trap, confirm the theoretical findings. A single model trained on several mini-apps generated by different reference methods captures all of them and remains stable up to twice the training time window, which points towards foundation models for fields in particle-based methods.

Abstract This study employs psychological network modeling to examine the interrelationships among science teachers’ perceptions of benefits, challenges, and attitudes toward integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools in science curriculum development. A total of 691 Saudi science teachers completed a validated questionnaire. Network estimation using regularization and centrality analyses identified key themes in science teachers’ perceptions of benefits, challenges, and attitudes toward integrating artificial intelligence (AI) tools into curriculum development and instructional practices. The estimated network revealed a dense structure. Centrality analyses indicated that curriculum content generation and innovative pedagogical tools were most central, while data processing challenges and algorithmic bias emerged as prominent structural barriers. Centrality metrics identify AI-facilitated curriculum design and innovative pedagogical tools as primary benefits, while challenges such as data processing limitations and algorithmic biases emerge as significant barriers. Teacher attitudes demonstrate ambivalence, characterized by resistance to automating administrative functions alongside guarded optimism for interactive and adaptive learning applications. These insights underscore the imperative to address technical constraints, ethical considerations, and the evolving professional identities of educators to ensure effective AI integration. The study contributes a nuanced, systemic understanding that informs the development of tailored AI tools and support frameworks, ultimately advancing transformative innovation in science education.

The conventional Artificial Intelligence (AI) has been observed to have challenges regarding interpretability and generalization when deployed in complex reasoning tasks. This setback diminishes its effectiveness in critical domains where such characteristics are required. Therefore, there has been a shift towards Neurosymbolic Artificial Intelligence (NeSyAI) to offer syntheses of neural network systems and symbolic reasoning inference. Basically, NeSyAI amalgamates symbolic thinking and deep learning through the leveraging of their synergy. As such, NeSyAI-based synthesis has been noted to be a promising paradigm that has seen an improvement in robustness, interpretability, and trustworthiness. In addition, it has capabilities of learning through comparatively small datasets. In a nutshell, the objective of neuro-symbolic reasoning is the combination of the ability to perceive and the ability to engage in logical inference. It also amalgamates deep learning with commonsense knowledge, which is a crucial requirement for intuitive visual analogy and semantically rich scene description. In this chapter, we provide some critical insights into NeSyAI, identify taxonomies, frameworks, domain-specific applications, and critical analyses of various emerging frontiers in this domain. In addition, we identify some critical research gaps in this field, which future research works can leverage on.

Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is increasingly used to extend clinical oversight into the home, particularly for people living with chronic disease. Connectivity alone does not make monitoring clinically useful: readings must be trustworthy, interpreted against the individual patient, routed to the right person, and acted upon. This focused narrative review examines intelligent RPM for home healthcare across connected themes: care-delivery evidence, physiological and activity sensing, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), physiological anomaly detection, alerting and alarm fatigue, clinical decisionsupport, medication adherence, patient–caregiver–clinician collaboration, and security, interoperability, and reliability. Literature was identified through ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, PubMed, JMIR, and Crossref-indexed IEEE and other publisher records, with emphasis on work published from 2020 to 2026. The evidence indicates that structured RPM can benefit selected opulations, but effects vary across conditions and outcomes. Algorithm studies often report strong retrospective performance, whereas evaluated RPM interventions still rely mostly on heuristic thresholds, and few validated algorithms have been tested in clinical trials. Baseline-relative detection on wearable data has shown promise in large cohort studies, while signal artefact, false alerts, limited external validation, and weak integration of adherence and caregiver roles remain unresolved. The review identifies the comparison between generic fixed thresholds and personalized temporal models, evaluated under realistic data-quality and alert-burden conditions, as a central open question. Future home-health platforms should combine quality-aware sensing, transparent safety rules, individualized trend analysis, tiered role-aware alerting, and clinician oversight.

Cotton ( Gossypium spp.) is a globally important fibre and oilseed crop whose productivity and quality are increasingly constrained by climate change, biotic stresses and the complex genetic architecture of key agronomic traits. Recent advances in genomics, high-throughput phenotyping and systems biology have transformed our understanding of cotton evolution, fibre development, stress adaptation and defence mechanisms. This review synthesizes current progress in cotton improvement through integrative approaches encompassing pan-genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, proteomics, metabolomics and phenomics, with particular emphasis on fibre quality regulation, secondary metabolite-mediated insect resistance and abiotic stress tolerance. We highlight how polyploidy, structural variation, homoeolog expression bias and regulatory network rewiring underpin phenotypic diversity and environmental adaptability in cotton. Furthermore, we discuss the emerging roles of artificial intelligence and machine-learning models in genomic prediction, trait mapping and decision support for precision breeding. The review also examines translational innovations, including CRISPR-based genome editing, nano-enabled delivery systems and nano-formulated inputs for sustainable pest and nutrient management. By integrating multi-omics data with AI-driven analytics, we propose a next-generation framework for accelerating cotton breeding pipelines under changing agro-ecological conditions. Despite rapid progress in Genomics, Bioinformatics, and Plant Breeding, existing reviews lack a systems-level perspective that links data generation, predictive modeling, and targeted intervention. This review addresses this gap by conceptualizing these advances as components of an integrated, data-driven breeding pipeline. This review uniquely integrates multi-omics and AI-driven approaches into a unified framework for cotton improvement, highlighting existing gaps and future opportunities. By integrating genome editing, nano-enabled delivery systems, and predictive analytics, these approaches enhance selection accuracy, reduce generation intervals, and enable high-throughput screening, collectively improving breeding efficiency, reduces breeding cycles and field-level resilience.

Grant’s (2013)provocative work popularized the “ambivert advantage,” the notion that those in the middle of the introversion-extraversion continuum perform better in sales positions. We contend that ambiverts outperform in sales only when face-to-face communication is minimal, such as in Grant’s (2013) outbound call center study. We argue that extraverts will outperform in face-to-face sales because of their greater ability to decode nonverbal signals, process working memory when multitasking, and interpret subtle signals between others. In analyses with 363 pharmaceutical salespeople and with 277 health-wine sales representatives, we find evidence that the extraversion—performance relation takes an inverted-U shape among sellers who had limited face-to-face customer interactions and a significant, linear, and positive relation when face-to-face interaction with customers was high. These studies refine recent thinking and provide a novel, nuanced view of personality and job design among salespeople that can be used to develop selection batteries and to craft jobs better matching worker strengths.

This article proposes that the theoretical framework of ‘metamodernism’ as defined by Vermeulen and van den Akker (2010) is becoming less and less suited to capturing the present cultural, political, social and artistic moment. Following their own framework in establishing the shift from postmodernism to metamodernism, this article suggests a similar shift is taking place and provisionally dubs the coming cultural paradigm ‘technobarbarism.’ Its defining characteristics are: political, economic, cultural and aesthetic polarisation, sensibilities shaped by generative AI and algorithmic standardisation, cynicism brought about by the breakdown of the global rules-based order and by an epistemic crisis, return to absurdism as a coping mechanism, de-contextualisation of prior work into short-form content, the second death of the author, the abandoning of the image of the artist as the ideal worker, nihilism and disillusionment with digital platforms, as well as an ever-growing demand for authenticity.

Methods for improving the safety of nuclear energy production and use facilities, including nuclear power plants (NPP) and other large industrial facilities in various countries, are presented and discussed. According to Concern «Rosenergoatom» data, the operation of all 10 Russian nuclear power plants (NPPs) was analyzed in details. The risks to the population in the region of each NPP were assessed when new reactors are commissioned under the Federal Purposed Program (FPP) for the intensive development of the Russian nuclear energy industry until 2021. It was determined that all of them comply with permissible sanitary standards. Their background radiation levels do not exceed natural one. Measures were proposed to reduce the likelihood of uncontrolled chaos, strengthen favorable social dynamics and the human factor in preventing both natural and man-made disasters. In the context of the rapidly changing global political situation, several possible methods of protection against targeted terrorist attacks and unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) used for these purposes. It was determined that all of them comply with the permissible sanitary standards. Their background radiation levels do not exceed natural levels. Measures were proposed to reduce the likelihood of uncontrolled chaos, strengthen favorable social dynamics, and utilize the human factor in preventing both natural and man-made disasters. In the context of the rapidly changing global political situation, some several possible methods of protection against targeted terrorist attacks and drones used for these purposes were proposed. These methods reduce the likelihood of uncontrolled chaos and enhance favorable social dynamics and the human factor in preventing both natural and man-madе possible disasters.

documents.abstract: Occupational heat exposure represents an important health and safety concern in the sugar manufacturing industry, where workers may experience prolonged exposure to heat generated by boilers, evaporation processes, and production machinery. Excessive heat exposure, particularly when combined with physical workload and inadequate fluid replacement, may increase the risk of dehydration and heat-related illness. This study aimed to assess occupational heat exposure conditions, existing workplace control measures, and dehydration prevention practices at a sugar manufacturing facility in Lampung, Indonesia. A descriptive qualitative approach was employed using workplace observations, field surveys, interviews with workers and company representatives, and a review of available occupational health and safety information. The assessment focused on production and boiler areas, perceived heat exposure, worker-reported symptoms, ventilation systems, personal protective equipment, drinking water availability, rest arrangements, and occupational health services. The findings were analyzed descriptively to identify existing preventive measures and potential gaps in workplace heat-stress management. The production and boiler areas were identified as workplaces with substantial potential for heat exposure due to continuous operation of processing equipment and heat-generating machinery. The facility employed approximately 485 workers and operated through three daily shifts. Workers reported experiencing hot working conditions, thirst, excessive sweating, fatigue, and dizziness during work activities. Existing occupational health measures included ventilation systems, cooling fans, personal protective equipment, access to drinking water, designated rest areas, workplace safety procedures, periodic medical examinations, and a company health clinic with 24-hour medical personnel. However, objective Wet Bulb Globe Temperature (WBGT) measurements and a specific worker hydration monitoring program were not documented. Consequently, the magnitude of occupational heat exposure and the prevalence of dehydration could not be established. The findings identify potential occupational heat hazards and highlight the importance of strengthening heat-specific preventive practices within an existing occupational health and safety system. Although general workplace safety and healthcare facilities were available, systematic heat exposure assessment, worker hydration monitoring, targeted education, and exposure-appropriate work–rest arrangements require further attention. Integrating these measures into occupational health management may support more comprehensive heat-stress prevention in sugar manufacturing facilities. Further quantitative investigations are necessary to evaluate environmental heat exposure, hydration status, and the effectiveness of preventive interventions.

documents.abstract: Existing Machine learning (ML)/Deep Learning (DL) based android malware detection approaches suffer from a series of issues viz. Adversarial Robustness, Higher Computational Complexity, Data Scarcity and Imbalance, Explainability and Interpretation, Higher False Positives and Meta/Polymorphic Nature of Malware. Our focus in this research is on two aspects viz. (a) addressing the Explainability and Interpretation issue that typically the DL-based techniques suffer from and (b) optimisation. In this paper, we propose a CNN-based adware detection method that uses an Android permission-based dataset (MadDroid). We convert the dataset permissions into black and white images and use them to train the proposed CNN model. We use eXplainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) techniques to get SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values and use them to find the feature’s contribution in the prediction of our model. By following this, the number of features reduces from 440 to 144 key features. We apply statistical methods to analyse SHAP values and highlight the most significant features by training and testing our model on each reduced dataset. We systematically find out the important features using CNN and XAI, and we have maintained the sequence of permission in the image to maintain the same sequence as the original feature set.

While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.

Large language model serving is limited by facility power. Energy per token determines how many tokens a datacenter can serve, while a latency target bounds how quickly each user receives them. During decode, every weight is read from memory for every generated token. Batching amortizes this read across users but makes no individual user faster. Speculative decoding does: a drafter proposes several future tokens, and the target model verifies them in a single forward pass that reuses the same weight read. Because every drafted token must be verified whether or not it is accepted, the energy speculation saves depends on how many drafted tokens are accepted. This saving is hard to pin down. It varies across target models from different attention families and across drafting schemes, and it depends on the text being served. Every drafter we evaluate accepts fewer tokens on conversation than on code, and every trained drafter accepts fewer on Romansh, a low-resource language, than on English. We measure speculative decoding under production serving conditions (SGLang, CUDA graphs enabled) on H100 and H200 GPUs, at batch sizes up to 64 across 5 corpora. On dense models, verification, not drafting, dominates the energy cost. The saving shrinks as the batch grows, because batching has already shared the weight read that speculation would divide among the accepted tokens. At large batch sizes, block drafters push verification past the balance point between arithmetic and memory traffic into the compute-bound regime, where the saving becomes a loss, and a drafter with low acceptance raises energy per token. Meeting a tighter latency target with speculation then costs additional energy. Larger batches lower energy per token without speculation. Speculation adds to that saving only when acceptance is high, and on the model we tested it leaves little headroom for latency-preserving DVFS.

Mental health support remains difficult to access for many individuals because of cost, stigma, limited availability of professionals, geographical barriers, and hesitation in discussing personal concerns.Conversational Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly systems based on Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Large Language Models (LLMs), offers a potential supplementary channel through which users can communicate in natural language and receive basic emotional or informational support.However, mental health is a sensitive application area in which fluent responses alone are not sufficient: reliability, contextual understanding, empathy, privacy, safety, bias, emotional dependency, and appropriate referral to human professionals are important concerns.This paper reviews the development and application of conversational AI for mental health support and synthesizes the gaps identified in the reviewed literature.Based on these gaps, a conceptual framework is proposed that combines user-input analysis, conversational context, LLM-based response generation, safety validation, and supportive response or professional referral.The framework is evaluated conceptually using eight dimensions: response relevance, empathy, context awareness, reliability, safety, privacy, usability, and transparency.The paper emphasizes that conversational AI should function as a supportive technological tool rather than a replacement for qualified mental health professionals.
