documents.abstract: Learning can be viewed as a process of enculturation that involves coming to understand how to use culturally relevant tools. It follows that, if we want to make valid assessments of and for learning, we need to account for how students use those tools. Traditional assessment practices tend to privilege tools in the head over tools in the world. But simply allowing students access to external tools like generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) during assessments is not sufficient to ensure validity. Hutchins’ work suggests that open tools—those that make problem steps and solutions more visible—provide wide horizons of observation and, in turn, provide evidence that can be used to make and justify assessment claims. Learning analytics platforms are one way to open up tools and widen horizons. However, current versions break the connection between tools and the cultures they represent, pulling interactions out of their authentic context of use. This chapter proposes a potential solution: we can instrument authentic tools in ways that widen our horizon of observation and move us towards more authentic assessment of GenAI-assisted practices.

Conflict-free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs) enable real-time collaborative editing by allowing distributed participants to modify local copies of shared documents while ensuring eventual convergence. Although this architecture provides availability and synchronization benefits, it introduces significant operational security challenges when participants cannot be fully trusted. This presentation examines security limitations in CRDT-based collaborative editing systems, focusing on Yjs, Automerge, Loro, and associated synchronization infrastructures. Particular attention is given to the persistence of deleted sensitive information, document-level authorization constraints, client identity impersonation, synchronization failures caused by rejected operations, the potential loss of offline contributions, and limitations of participant revocation. The analysis incorporates technical demonstrations and reproducible experiments involving Yjs, Hocuspocus, y-websocket, and Durable Streams. These examples illustrate how malicious participants may manipulate operation identifiers, impersonate legitimate collaborators, and compromise the integrity of shared documents. A central contribution is the examination of artificial intelligence agents as active CRDT participants. The presentation demonstrates how AI-assisted editing can amplify existing authorization weaknesses through confused-deputy scenarios, excessive agency, and exposure to untrusted document content. It further discusses the implications of the Agents Rule of Two for collaborative AI systems. Practical security recommendations include separating untrusted content from editing privileges, introducing human review before applying AI-generated modifications, restricting agent capabilities through dedicated tools, assigning distinct agent identities, and implementing cryptographically verifiable operations. Fine-grained access control at the document-section level is also considered as a direction for improving collaborative editing security. The presentation highlights the need to integrate access control, identity verification, cryptographic integrity, and human oversight into the architecture of secure CRDT-based collaborative systems.

Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing the landscape of translation, expanding translators’ involvement in interaction configurations, evaluation of AI-generated outputs, and governance of risks within augmented translation environments. This study defines Human–AI Interaction in Translation (HAIT) as GenAI-mediated component of the human-centred augmented translation process, where GenAI is integrated into translation technologies and conversational large language models. Translation education lacks a developmental structure that connects these emerging requirements and their related digital competences to curriculum design. This study proposes a workflow-derived operationalisation of HAIT for translator education. A conceptual functional analysis of augmented translation workflows produced eight HAIT requirements, which were mapped to the 21 competences of the European Digital Competence Framework (DigComp 3.0) by assessing 168 potential relationships for functional correspondence, scope fidelity, and traceable justification. The analysis accepted 37 relationships among 16 competences and identified translation-specific residues that require curricular supplementation. The operationalised requirements were organised into a proposed four-level progression informed by DigComp proficiency levels. An exploratory mixed-methods pilot with 42 second-year translation students examined perceived relevance after contextualised exposure in a course-embedded intervention. Students broadly perceived DigComp as relevant to translation education and practice, particularly focusing on competences related to familiar topics such as privacy protection, device security, copyright, information retrieval, communication and collaboration, with limited attention to information evaluation and programming competences. Their responses were less explicit about AI-generated output evaluation, prompting and in-context steering, grounding configuration, and risk-responsive actions, highlighting the value of a spiral curriculum for competence development and Quality Education (SDG4).

Agriculture is indispensable for the security of the global food supply; however, diseases that are often unnoticed in their initial stages cause a considerable decline in crop yield. Manual disease detection via traditional means is slow, requires a lot of manpower, and can result in mistakes; thus, it is not appropriate for extensive or instantaneous diagnoses. This study proposes a refined Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) model tailored for reliable and automatic detection of plant diseases using images of leaves taken in the field under real-world agricultural conditions. A deep CNN that has been trained on a vast plant disease dataset shows impressive multi-class classification accuracy and at the same time, has low computational demands. Through a mobile or web interface, users can receive feedback that is nearly real-time; thus, it is affordable for farmers who use devices with low resources. The integration of artificial intelligence into the agricultural workflow has made the proposed methodology a scalable, cost-effective, and eco-friendly solution for the prompt detection of diseases and better crop management in the future.

Neurodegenerative disorders, including Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, Huntington's disease, amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, multiple sclerosis and stroke, are characterized by progressive neuronal dysfunction, synaptic impairment and neural circuit degeneration, leading to severe cognitive and motor deficits. Although considerable progress has been made in understanding their molecular pathology, the circuit level mechanisms driving disease onset and progression remain incompletely understood. Optogenetics, which combines microbial opsins, genetic engineering and optical stimulation, enables reversible, cell-specific control of neuronal activity with millisecond precision and has transformed neuroscience from observational analysis to causal investigation of neural circuits. This review summarizes recent advances in the molecular basis of optogenetics, microbial opsins, gene delivery strategies and optical stimulation technologies, together with their applications in basic neurobiology and neurodegenerative disease research. We discuss how optogenetics has advanced understanding of neural circuit organization, synaptic plasticity, memory, neurodevelopment, sleep regulation, protein aggregation, synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, mitochondrial impairment, oxidative stress and regulated cell death. Although these studies have generated important mechanistic insights and demonstrated functional improvements in experimental models, translation into human therapies remains investigational due to challenges associated with gene delivery, long-term opsin expression, immune compatibility and optical accessibility. Emerging therapeutic strategies, including closed-loop neuromodulation, wireless photostimulation, artificial intelligence-assisted neural decoding, nanotechnology enabled light delivery and brain computer interfaces, are critically evaluated with emphasis on their current evidence status, translational challenges and limitations for clinical implementation. Collectively, optogenetics provides an unprecedented platform for deciphering disease mechanisms and evaluating circuit-based neuromodulation strategies, while continued technological and biological validation will determine its future role in precision therapies for neurodegenerative disorders.

Organizations operate in complex environments shaped by stakeholders, institutions, regulations, technologies and societal expectations. Their ability to survive, adapt and create value depends not only on internal capabilities but also on their responses to external pressures and on maintaining legitimacy. Relationships among organizations, stakeholders and organizational environments shape organizational priorities, resource access and opportunities for action. Stakeholder theory, legitimacy and institutional perspectives offer important lenses for understanding how organizations gain support, secure resources and maintain their licence to operate. Governments, customers, employees, investors, communities and advocacy groups all influence organizational choices, often in different and competing ways. Broader environmental forces, including digitalization, artificial intelligence, sustainability challenges, globalization and regulatory change, create both opportunities and constraints. These developments generate new expectations, strategic dilemmas and pressures to adapt. Organizations are embedded within social, economic, political, technological and ecological systems, making context central to organizational analysis and practice.

Conventional notions of originality position university students as the sole authors of the work they submit for assessment. This means that originality is seen as a kind of academic alchemy, whereby students draw from other sources to complete their work but must somehow transform it into something that is wholly of themselves. In this chapter, we propose an alternative framing of originality—as a texture of contributions—to acknowledge the interwoven nature of how students produce work with artificial intelligence (AI). The key distinction is that students’ interactions with AI (or others) are understood as textural rather than absolute. In contrast to approaches which attempt to fully disentangle human and AI, this perspective reorients assessment design to consider two different foci for assurance: work and working . Most current assessment focuses on fixed outputs (work), whether interim or final, to assure achievement. However, this approach cannot assure students’ ways of working, which we argue requires assessors to be participants in the dynamic activity involved in generating work. By being participants in working, assessors can more fully understand the nature of students’ contributions to the work they submit for assessment, and so can make further assurances about the originality of that work.

This paper examines whether recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) and space-based military technologies have produced a paradigm shift in interstate conflict or have primarily enhanced the conduct of warfare within an existing strategic framework.Existing research has largely emphasized technological development and operational efficiency, while paying comparatively less attention to whether military innovation fundamentally transforms the strategic logic through which battlefield success is converted into strategic outcomes.To address this gap, the paper develops an analytical framework combining the concepts of paradigm shift, critical juncture, and military innovation.It distinguishes tactical and operational change from strategic transformation and argues that a paradigm shift occurs only when technological innovation becomes sufficiently institutionalized to generate a durable transformation in how wars are fought, won, and terminated.Using a qualitative comparative design, the study contrasts short-term decisive operations with prolonged conflicts and evaluates the effects of AI-enabled and space-based systems across both operational and strategic criteria.The findings show that these technologies substantially enhance surveillance, target identification, precision strike, command coordination, and battlespace awareness when objectives are limited and targets are identifiable in advance.Their strategic effects, however, diminish as conflicts become prolonged, when geography, manpower, industrial capacity, political resilience, and escalation management reassert their importance.It therefore argues that recent military innovation has produced substantial tactical and operational transformation without yet displacing the underlying strategic grammar of warfare.It academically contributes by providing a clearer analytical threshold for distinguishing military innovation from a genuine paradigm shift, while acknowledging that the recent and ongoing nature of the cases and reliance on publicly available qualitative evidence limit definitive conclusions about their longer-term strategic consequences.
topics: European and Russian Geopolitical Military Strategies

documents.abstract: Background: Cognitive workload classification from electroencephalography is affected by interindividual variability in EEG signals and subjective workload responses. We propose participant-specific adaptive label smoothing, in which the change in perceived workload between resting and task conditions controls the target confidence, while the experimental class remains unchanged. Methods: The method was evaluated on the STEW dataset and compared with five alternative supervision strategies. Two classification models were used: a feature-based convolutional neural network and a multi-scale Swin Transformer network (MST-Net) operating on time-frequency representations. Global and participant-specific stratified normalization were evaluated using participant-disjoint cross-validation. The participant-specific approach used normalization statistics estimated from each unseen participant’s own unlabeled EEG data. Results: Under stratified normalization, adaptive label smoothing produced the highest macro F1 for both models, with values of 0.768 and 0.796, and ROC AUC values of 0.844 and 0.878, respectively. It also maintained high recall for both classes. Conclusions: The findings suggest that participant-specific subjective workload responses can be used to modulate target confidence, with the most consistent benefit observed under participant-specific normalization. As the strategies differ in target definitions and no hard rest/task or fixed label-smoothing control was evaluated, the differences are descriptive.

Medical AI learns from the answers doctors record, but rarely from how they interpret the evidence to reach them. Here we introduce PathCowork, a framework that turns pathologists' narrated examinations into supervision for visual grounding and procedures that guide diagnostic AI agents. Synchronized gaze, narration and navigation link visual findings to the process of interpreting them. Across 48 sessions from 16 pathologists, the platform captured 1,028 minutes of slide review. Using these data, we trained PathCowork-1T for server deployment and PathCowork-27B for local deployment, with improved visual grounding. Across five organ-specific evaluations, agents combining this grounding with recorded diagnostic procedures achieved primary task scores averaging 17.9 and 24.1 percentage points higher than Claude Code and Codex, respectively, with shorter processing times and lower inference costs. Compared to the state-of-the-art multiple-instance learning AIs, the PathCowork agent-proposed regions achieved higher prostate-grading scores with limited slide labels. PathCowork can also help construct pathology AI benchmarks where questions derived from the recordings identified difficulties in recognizing viewing context and rejecting inapplicable premises. In summary, PathCowork proposes a new paradigm to scale up the data collection and train pathology AI through transparent reasoning from diagnostic sessions, opening a path towards systems that learn directly from routine clinical practice.

documents.abstract: When one AI agent tells another that "the tests passed" or "a person approved this refund", the receiver has only the sender's word. A2A and MCP authenticate the channel, but the sender is the party in doubt, so a prompt-injected agent can launder fabricated facts and authority through a multi-agent system. We present Proof-Carrying Messages (PCM), a protocol in which each claim carries evidence: records from an append-only Merkle log that the agent cannot write, with inclusion proofs, signed by an attesting signer the agent cannot control. Receivers check messages offline and give each claim a three-valued result: proven, unproven or failed. A claim that rests only on the agent's own report is never proven. Authority travels as grant chains rooted in a recorded human approval, and the chains can only narrow. We specify four claim types, a typed caveat algebra, replay rules that survive restarts, and strict readings that make independent verifiers agree, and we prove the resulting security properties. On a pre-specified benchmark of 926 messages from real runs, 712 of them lies in 16 classes, PCM accepts 10 lies, all of them stale evidence (1.4%, 95% CI 0.8-2.6%). Plain A2A accepts all 712, and models of six deployed protocols (A2A with signed Agent Cards, uAgents, RFC 9421, SCITT, AP2, Verifiable Intent) accept 504-712. Two independent verifiers agree on all 926 verdicts, and verification takes about 1 ms.

In Türkiye, pediatricians’ perspectives on artificial intelligence (AI), including their knowledge, trust, and concerns, remain underexplored. This study aims to evaluate pediatricians’ knowledge, perceptions, and acceptance of AI in pediatric care. A cross-sectional, open, web-based convenience survey was conducted among pediatricians in Türkiye, including residents and specialists. The survey assessed their knowledge of AI, perceptions of its benefits and risks, and acceptance of AI as a clinical decision support tool. A total of 403 pediatricians accessed the survey; 18 declined to participate, 1 was excluded for a completion time under two minutes, and 16 were excluded for an inconsistent control-item. After excluding responses, 368 were included in the analysis. Participants had a median age of 35 years and a median of 9 years of pediatric care experience. Only 9.5% of participants reported awareness of AI in pediatrics, and 85.9% rated their self-perceived AI knowledge as average or below. Despite this, 74.2% agreed that AI will improve pediatrics, and 88.3% stated it could enhance care quality. Concerns included legal liability (78.5%), data security (54.6%), and the black-box nature of AI (59.2%). Across all 37 ordinal items, a single age correlation survived: younger respondents were more likely to expect AI to increase diagnostic confidence (r s = -0.171, 95% CI -0.269 to -0.070, small effect size; P = 0.001; P adj = 0.038). While 90.8% supported AI as a clinical decision support tool, only 17.4% believed AI could replace human physicians in non-invasive roles. Only 19.3% expected their institution to allocate financial or personnel resources for AI integration. Survey respondents generally view AI as a promising tool to improve pediatric care but express significant concerns about its reliability, ethical implications, and legal responsibilities.

documents.abstract: The development of artificial intelligence in education opens up opportunities to support learning while also raising ethical issues related to academic integrity and students’ digital responsibility. This article aims to analyze the role of character education as a foundation for guiding the use of artificial intelligence in relation to these two aspects. The study employs a literature review using a descriptive-qualitative approach. The findings indicate that the values of ṣidq and amanah provide a conceptual foundation for transparency in AI use, recognition of intellectual contributions, adherence to assignment guidelines, and accountability for learning processes and outcomes. Meanwhile, the values of tabayyun, respect for others, and a focus on the common good underpin digital responsibility in the form of information verification, privacy protection, respect for intellectual property, and consideration of the social impacts of AI use. Strengthening these two aspects requires educators to lead by example, clear institutional guidelines, family support, and reflective learning grounded in ethical dilemmas. This article concludes that the integration of character education and AI literacy should be directed toward developing students who are proficient in using technology while also being able to make decisions honestly and responsibly. The resulting conceptual framework still requires empirical testing according to educational levels and contexts.

Teachers' competence in designing technology-based interactive learning media is one of the key factors for successful 21st-century learning. However, initial mapping at SMP Plus Aisyah Samawa revealed that approximately 70% of teachers still relied on conventional learning media, and more than 80% were unfamiliar with the Artificial Intelligence (AI) features of the Canva design platform, such as Magic Design, AI Presentation, and Text to Image. This community service program aimed to strengthen teachers' technical and pedagogical competence in developing interactive learning media using Canva AI, integrated with lesson plans (RPP) or teaching modules. The program was implemented in three stages: preparation, implementation (socialization, hands-on training with a 30% theory–70% practice composition, and classroom technology application), and evaluation, supported by three months of intensive post-training mentoring. Program success indicators were measured through pretest–posttest score improvements, the percentage of teachers producing interactive learning media products, and the integration of such media into lesson plans or teaching modules. The results showed an improvement in teachers' competence in utilizing Canva's AI features and an increase in student engagement during the learning process. This program is expected to serve as a replicable model for strengthening teachers' digital literacy in other pesantren-based schools in Sumbawa Regency, while contributing to the achievement of SDG 4 (Quality Education) and SDG 9 (Industry, Innovation, and Infrastructure).

Purpose: This study aimed to design and develop furniture as a medium or assistive tool to foster children’s disciplined behavior in returning their belongings to designated places at home. Methodology: The study employed an ergonomic product design approach integrated with a biomimicry design method. Findings: The study produced a piece of furniture whose form and colors resemble the fruit of the Patuk Manuk plant (Thunbergia alata). Observations indicated that the product created an enjoyable experience for children when placing their belongings neatly and systematically. The System Usability Scale (SUS) yielded a score of 80, indicating good usability, while the Godspeed questionnaire demonstrated high reliability, with a Cronbach’s alpha of 0.93. Conclusion: The study developed an ergonomic assistive product that supports the development of disciplined behavior in children. The product demonstrated good usability, was well accepted by both children and parents, and provided an enjoyable experience for users interacting with it. Originality: The design integrates ergonomic product design and biomimicry, a combination that remains relatively uncommon in innovative product development. Integrating these approaches is expected to provide complementary benefits in developing learning aids that support the formation of disciplined habits among children in the home environment.

This study systematically reviews the literature on the relationships between individuals' perceptions of artificial intelligence, naturalistic decision-making and cognitive flexibility, and synthesizes the evidence into an integrated model in which cognitive flexibility mediates the effect of artificial intelligence perceptions on naturalistic decision-making. Following the PRISMA 2020 statement, three Boolean searches corresponding to the pairwise relationships were run in OpenAlex on 20 October 2026 and complemented by backward and forward citation tracking. Of 1,161 records identified, 1,140 were screened, 99 were assessed in full and 70 met the eligibility criteria; together with 32 studies reached through citation tracking, 102 studies were coded and synthesized thematically. The synthesis shows that the three constructs have been studied in largely separate streams: research on artificial intelligence and decision-making concentrates on advice-taking, reliance and decision-making styles; research on artificial intelligence and cognitive flexibility is very recent, concentrated in educational and health settings and consistent in sign; and research on cognitive flexibility and decision-making draws on laboratory, neurophysiological and survey evidence. Cognitive flexibility is a replicated mediator in adjacent domains, but no study has tested the full chain from artificial intelligence perceptions through cognitive flexibility to naturalistic decision-making. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, Cognitive Load Theory, Cognitive Flexibility Theory and the recognition-primed decision model, the study formulates four testable propositions, presents an integrated model, identifies measurement options and outlines a research agenda.

Images reveal appearances, but counting often asks about physical objects. A single entity may be visible directly, in several reflections, or through glass, so detecting every visible occurrence does not determine how many entities are present. Existing visual counting benchmarks rarely separate these two operations. We introduce PhysCount, a benchmark for evaluating whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can distinguish what appears in an image from what physically exists in the scene. PhysCount contains 546 real-world images and 4,595 human-written questions organized into 651 target-specific groups. For each group, annotators locate the relevant appearances, label how each is observed, and identify appearances of the same entity. Four complementary question families test the enumeration of appearances, the enumeration of physical entities, image-formation-specific counting, and appearance--entity correspondence. We measure both accuracy on each family and the proportion of groups answered entirely correctly. Across 40 MLLMs, counting visible appearances is substantially easier than recovering the identities that connect them. Even the strongest model answers every question correctly in only 13.36\% of groups. Performance declines when one entity produces many appearances or when its appearances cross observation modes. Higher image resolution improves access to visual evidence but brings limited gains in complete-group accuracy, whereas answering related questions jointly produces a marked improvement. These results expose a gap between recognizing what is visible and correctly recovering the physical entities behind those observations.

documents.abstract: Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems (RPAS) operations are expected to increase traffic complexity in terminal-area airspace, creating new challenges for tactical separation assurance and pilot decision-making. This study evaluated subjective pilot responses to the latest version of the Airborne Collision Avoidance System for rotorcraft (ACAS Xr) during simulated RPAS operations in approach, departure, and en-route conditions. Eleven IFR-rated fixed-wing pilots completed simulated flight scenarios using ACAS Xr, including encounters involving cooperative and non-cooperative traffic and dynamic terminal-area logic. Subjective measures were collected and included workload, usability, and operational acceptability. Pilots rated ACAS Xr positively for guidance effectiveness, safe separation support, and traffic-symbol clarity for aircraft equipped and not equipped with Automatic Dependent Surveillance-Broadcast. However, terminal-area warning alerts were sometimes perceived as untimely or operationally inappropriate, particularly Level Off and Descend advisories. Results support continued development of ACAS Xr while highlighting areas requiring refinement for terminal-area operations.

Precision medicine is an emerging healthcare paradigm that tailors prevention, diagnosis, and treatment to individual patients using genetic, clinical, environmental, and lifestyle information. Advances in next-generation sequencing, bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence (AI) now allow clinicians to analyse genomic variants, stratify disease risk, and select therapies at a level of individual detail that population-averaged medicine cannot provide. This paper reviews AI-enabled precision medicine, synthesising landmark and recent peer-reviewed literature published between 2004 and 2026, and tracing the field from early blood-group stratification through the Human Genome Project to national precision medicine programmes and the multimodal AI of the present day. A conceptual framework is proposed that integrates electronic health records, genomic sequencing, laboratory tests, and wearable-device data in a secure platform where AI models identify biomarkers, predict risk, and recommend treatment for clinician validation; it is synthesised from literature-reported practices rather than experimentally validated. Applications in oncology, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, rare genetic disorders, pharmacogenomics, and remote monitoring are examined, followed by the main challenges, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, unrepresentative genomic datasets, cost, interpretability, and ethics, together with mitigation strategies. Emerging directions, including digital twins, federated learning, multimodal AI, and CRISPR-assisted therapies, are discussed. This review highlights the role of AI and genomics in moving healthcare from reactive to predictive and personalised, and identifies priorities for future research.
